paragraphs: A diffusion model can produce appealing images while still occasionally generating outputs that people do not want. This paper studies that particular situation: a pretrained generator already has useful capabilities, but its output only partly matches human preferences. The authors call the task of preventing those undesirable generations censoring.

Their approach uses a reward model trained with a small amount of human feedback to support censored generation from the pretrained diffusion model. The feedback supplies judgments about desirable and undesirable outputs. This gives the censoring process a learned signal for distinguishing acceptable images from the unwanted part of the generator’s output.

The reported finding is that labels collected through only a few minutes of human feedback can be sufficient for this task. Its significance is the small human effort needed to address partial misalignment in the studied setting. The result concerns censoring an already capable generator; it does not establish that a few minutes of feedback can resolve every kind of mismatch between image generation and human preferences.
neurips-2023-censored-sampling-of-diffus.tldr: A reward model learned from a few minutes of human feedback can support suppressing unwanted outputs from an already capable diffusion model.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a distinctive structure that appears in a network’s final layer late in training. Experiments have also found related structure in earlier layers, a phenomenon called deep neural collapse. Explaining that multilayer pattern is harder: earlier theoretical work addressed linear layers or only the final two layers with an additional assumption.

The paper extends the unconstrained features model, an existing framework for analyzing neural collapse, to multiple nonlinear layers. Within this deep version of the framework, the authors prove that the unique global optimum for binary classification has the properties associated with deep neural collapse. The binary classification setting and the analytical model are essential to the scope of this result.

Two empirical checks support the theory. Gradient descent on the deep unconstrained features model produces solutions that agree well with the prediction, and trained networks recover features suitable for deep neural collapse. Together, these findings connect the mathematical framework to observed network behavior and support its use in explaining why collapse can extend beyond the final layer.
neurips-2023-deep-neural-collapse-is-pro.tldr: For binary classification in a deep unconstrained features model, the authors prove that the unique global optimum exhibits deep neural collapse.

paragraphs: People can disagree about whether a conversational AI response is safe, and those judgments can depend on social and cultural context. Reducing every example to a single positive or negative label can hide that disagreement. DICES is a dataset designed to make differences in safety perception visible and measurable.

The dataset combines detailed demographic information about raters with many ratings for each item. It represents votes as distributions across demographic groups, preserving how judgments vary instead of retaining only an aggregate verdict. The repeated ratings provide statistical support for analysis, while the distributions let researchers examine different ways of combining individual opinions.

The authors also describe metrics showing how rater diversity affects safety judgments across geographic regions, ethnicities, ages, and genders. This makes DICES useful for examining ambiguity and differences that a single overall score can obscure. Its contribution is a shared evaluation resource that supports analysis of multiple perspectives, helping researchers assess conversational AI safety while retaining the diversity of the people making those assessments.
neurips-2023-dices-dataset-diversity-in-.tldr: DICES preserves demographic variation and disagreement in human ratings so conversational AI safety can be evaluated across diverse perspectives.

paragraphs: Graph dataset distillation creates a smaller synthetic graph to reduce training and storage costs. The authors argue that existing approaches emphasize node features while neglecting the original graph’s connectivity. Their spectral analysis identifies substantial shifts in Laplacian Energy Distribution, or LED, associated with poor transfer across architectures and weaker anomaly detection and link prediction.

Their method, Structure-broadcasting Graph Dataset Distillation, carries original structural information into synthetic graph generation. This explicitly addresses the part of the graph that feature-focused condensation can overlook. The theoretical analysis indicates that the resulting graphs are expected to have smaller LED shifts than earlier methods, connecting structural preservation to downstream performance.

Experiments across nine datasets report state-of-the-art results and LED shift reductions between 17.6% and 31.4%. On YelpChi, the distilled graph retains 98.6% of the test accuracy obtained with the original graph while reducing graph scale by a factor of 1,000. That percentage describes retained performance relative to the original training result, rather than an absolute test accuracy of 98.6%.
neurips-2023-does-graph-distillation-see.tldr: SGDD preserves original graph structure during distillation, reducing spectral shifts and improving performance across architectures and graph tasks.

paragraphs: Neural methods for vehicle routing can perform well when new problems resemble their training examples, yet struggle when the distribution of routing instances changes. This paper addresses that generalization problem by learning several routing sub-policies through deep reinforcement learning. The group is intended to cope with a variety of instance distributions.

The central design issue is keeping those sub-policies meaningfully different. Simply training several policies can allow their parameters to converge toward the same solution. The authors combine bootstrap training with random initialization to encourage diversity, then add regularization terms that explicitly promote differences between policies. Both mechanisms serve the same goal: maintaining useful variety within the ensemble.

In experiments, the method outperforms state-of-the-art neural baselines on randomly generated instances from multiple distributions. It also generalizes favorably to benchmark instances from TSPLib and CVRPLib. The reported results support both the overall ensemble approach and its individual diversity mechanisms, suggesting that deliberately varied routing policies can help address the distribution changes tested in the study.
neurips-2023-ensemble-based-deep-reinfor.tldr: An ensemble of deliberately diverse reinforcement learning policies improves vehicle routing performance under the distribution shifts tested.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train a shared model without exchanging their local datasets. Compromised clients can nevertheless introduce a backdoor, causing inputs with a particular trigger to receive an attacker-chosen prediction. Defenses that detect and exclude suspicious contributions using a fixed attacker model can struggle when attackers strategically change their behavior.

FedGame treats this interaction as a minimax game between the defender and adaptive attackers. The authors use analysis of that game to design an interactive defense mechanism. This makes strategic adaptation part of the defense problem, rather than treating malicious behavior as a fixed pattern that only needs to be identified.

The paper provides a conditional theoretical guarantee: under assumptions described as mild, the model trained with FedGame during backdoor attacks remains close to the model trained without attacks. Experiments on several benchmark datasets and attacks report substantially stronger robustness than the compared defenses. These findings support the approach against the strategic attackers studied, while the theoretical closeness result retains its stated assumptions.
neurips-2023-fedgame-a-game-theoretic-de.tldr: FedGame models adaptive backdoor attackers and a federated learning defender as a minimax game, yielding conditional guarantees and improved empirical robustness.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large language models with backpropagation can require far more memory than running them for inference. MeZO addresses this by estimating updates through forward passes and adapting a classical zeroth-order optimization method to operate in place. The result is fine-tuning with the same memory footprint as inference.

The practical difference is substantial in the reported example: one A100 with 80GB of memory supports training a 30-billion-parameter model with MeZO, compared with a 2.7-billion-parameter model using backpropagation. Experiments cover masked and autoregressive models, sizes up to 66 billion parameters, and classification, multiple-choice, and generation tasks.

MeZO outperforms in-context learning and linear probing, and matches backpropagation-based fine-tuning performance on multiple tasks. The implementation achieves reductions of up to twelvefold in memory and twofold in GPU-hours. It also supports full-parameter tuning, LoRA, prefix tuning, and objectives such as accuracy or F1 that are not differentiable. The accompanying theory highlights adequate pretraining and task prompts as factors helping explain why this approach can work despite pessimistic classical analyses.
neurips-2023-fine-tuning-language-models.tldr: MeZO fine-tunes language models using forward passes with inference-level memory, achieving performance comparable to backpropagation on multiple tested tasks.

paragraphs: Mixup trains neural networks on combinations of examples to encourage smoother decision boundaries. Dynamic mixup methods improve these combinations by emphasizing relevant image regions, but optimizing mixed examples against their labels adds computation. This paper questions whether that extra optimization is always useful: a mismatch between a mixed example and its label can itself provide an informative training challenge.

The authors introduce decoupled mixup, or DM, which changes the training objective through a decoupled regularizer. Its purpose is to use difficult mixed examples adaptively to identify discriminative features while retaining mixup’s smoothing effect. The method therefore addresses two aspects of learning together: keeping boundaries smooth and recognizing the features that distinguish classes.

Experiments cover supervised and semi-supervised learning across seven datasets. The reported results show that DM lets static mixup methods match or sometimes exceed dynamic methods without additional computation. The broader implication is that improving how a model learns from mixed examples can be effective without making the process for constructing those examples more complicated.
neurips-2023-harnessing-hard-mixed-sampl.tldr: Decoupled mixup uses difficult mixed examples to learn discriminative features while preserving smooth decision boundaries and avoiding extra computation.

paragraphs: Detecting three-dimensional objects from point clouds is difficult because the points are sparsely distributed. Efficient sparse convolutional networks often use operations that prevent disconnected spatial features from exchanging information. That restriction can make it harder to combine evidence spread across a scene, particularly for large objects or objects far from the sensor.

HEDNet addresses this with a hierarchy of encoder-decoder blocks that captures dependencies between features over longer spatial distances. The architectural choice targets the information-sharing problem created by sparse inputs. The authors position it against approaches using larger convolution kernels or self-attention, which had offered limited accuracy improvements or required excessive computation.

Experiments on the Waymo Open and nuScenes datasets report better detection accuracy than previous state-of-the-art methods while maintaining competitive efficiency. The result supports using hierarchical encoder-decoder processing to connect spatially separated evidence in point clouds. Its contribution is an accuracy and efficiency combination demonstrated on those two datasets, with particular motivation from the difficulty of representing large and distant objects.
neurips-2023-hednet-a-hierarchical-encod.tldr: HEDNet connects spatially separated point-cloud features through hierarchical encoder-decoder blocks, improving 3D detection accuracy with competitive efficiency.

paragraphs: Monocular depth estimation predicts distance from a single image. Some methods divide possible depths into bins and combine bin centers with predicted probabilities to obtain a depth estimate. IEBins develops this approach into a sequence of increasingly detailed searches, progressively refining the range in which a depth value is sought.

At each stage, the method searches more finely within a target bin selected from the preceding stage. An early mistake could otherwise constrain later searches to an unsuitable range. To alleviate that accumulation of error, IEBins makes the target bin elastic: its width changes according to depth uncertainty. This lets the refinement process account for uncertainty rather than treating every intermediate estimate as equally reliable.

The framework combines a feature extractor with a GRU-based iterative optimizer that models context across refinement stages. Experiments on KITTI, NYU-Depth-v2, and SUN RGB-D report performance beyond prior state-of-the-art competitors. These findings support uncertainty-adjusted search ranges as a useful way to refine depth predictions while addressing the errors that can accumulate during iterative estimation.
neurips-2023-iebins-iterative-elastic-bi.tldr: IEBins refines depth estimates through progressively finer searches whose bin widths adapt to uncertainty, improving results on three depth-estimation datasets.

paragraphs: Im-Promptu investigates whether visual demonstrations can communicate composition rules through analogy. The authors introduce three benchmarks for testing visual in-context generalization and formalize an analogy-based learner. They then build a meta-learning framework around that formulation, asking how the representation of an image affects what a learner can infer from examples.

The study compares representations at different levels: whole vectors, image patches, and object slots. This matters because the units a model receives determine which visual elements it can readily combine. The experiments reveal tradeoffs: non-compositional representations can extend learned rules to unseen domains, yet struggle on tasks requiring new combinations of elements.

Patch representations need patches containing entire objects for robust extrapolation in the reported experiments. Object-centered tokenization combined with cross-attention produces consistent, high-fidelity solutions, with these design choices especially important for compositional generalization. The paper also demonstrates Im-Promptu as an image-generation programming interface. Together, the results link the usefulness of visual prompts to whether a model’s representational units align with the elements being composed.
neurips-2023-im-promptu-in-context-compo.tldr: Im-Promptu studies learning visual composition from examples and finds that object-centered representations with cross-attention particularly support compositional generalization.

paragraphs: NetHack remains a challenging setting for reinforcement learning, with learned methods still trailing rule-based solutions. Learning from previously collected gameplay is a promising direction. Although a large NetHack dataset already exists, the authors argue that access to data alone has not been enough to encourage broad adoption by the offline reinforcement learning community.

Katakomba addresses three obstacles: tools, implementations, and benchmarks. Its open-source library provides predefined tasks in a style familiar from D4RL, straightforward baseline implementations, and evaluation tools. Accompanying configurations and logs are synchronized to the cloud, providing supporting records alongside the code and task definitions.

The contribution is a more complete workflow for studying learning from existing NetHack data. Researchers receive defined problems to work on, starting implementations, and infrastructure for evaluating results, rather than needing to assemble each component around the dataset themselves. The paper presents this infrastructure as a way to make data-driven NetHack research more accessible and comparable, supporting investigation of whether offline reinforcement learning can help close the gap with rule-based play.
neurips-2023-katakomba-tools-and-benchma.tldr: Katakomba supplies tasks, baseline implementations, and evaluation infrastructure to make offline reinforcement learning research on NetHack easier to conduct.

paragraphs: Finding optimal auction rules is difficult even in relatively simple settings. Neural networks have nevertheless shown an ability to recover known optimal mechanisms and discover new ones. This paper seeks theoretical insight into that empirical success by examining the shape of the optimization problem for networks used to design auctions.

The authors study RochetNet and a generalized network for affine maximizer auctions. They prove a property called mode connectivity: locally optimal solutions can be joined by a simple piecewise linear path, and every solution along that path is almost as good as one of the two endpoint optima. The statement concerns the quality of connecting paths; it does not identify every local optimum as globally optimal.

Mode connectivity had already attracted attention in networks used for prediction. This work brings that analysis into differentiable economics, where networks directly solve non-convex optimization problems. The result provides a structural explanation relevant to auction-learning success: good solutions in these studied models are connected through paths that preserve the stated level of solution quality.
neurips-2023-mode-connectivity-in-auctio.tldr: The authors prove that local optima in two neural auction-design models are connected by piecewise linear paths with controlled solution quality.

paragraphs: Training a neural network one module at a time is attractive when memory is limited, including on-device settings. However, greedy training can stagnate: early layers overfit, and adding deeper layers eventually stops improving test accuracy. This paper introduces a regularizer intended to keep successive modules making useful progress.

The method is called Transport Regularized Greedy Learning, or TRGL. Its module-wise regularization is inspired by the minimizing movement scheme, a mathematical approach associated with gradient flows over distributions. The theoretical analysis proves that the resulting greedy modules have regularity properties and progressively solve the task, giving a mathematical basis for the proposed remedy to stagnation.

Experiments add the regularizer to module-wise training of ResNets, Transformers, and VGG architectures. The authors report improved accuracy over other module-wise methods and, often, over end-to-end training, with memory reductions reaching 60%. These results suggest that regulating how individual modules learn can make memory-saving training more effective, while the comparison with end-to-end training remains an outcome that occurs often rather than universally.
neurips-2023-module-wise-training-of-neu.tldr: TRGL adds transport-inspired regularization to greedy module-wise training, improving accuracy and reporting memory savings of up to 60%.

paragraphs: Bayesian decision-making uses uncertainty about a model to choose an action. This paper studies a risk-sensitive version that replaces the usual posterior expectation of loss with an entropic risk measure. The computational challenge is that the posterior itself may be intractable, as often happens with large datasets and complex models.

The authors use a dual representation of the risk measure to construct risk-sensitive variational Bayes, or RSVB. The framework jointly computes an approximation to the posterior and the associated decision rule. This connects the approximation process directly to the risk-sensitive decision problem. It also includes loss-calibrated variational Bayes as a special case.

The analysis examines how these computational approximations affect the predictive performance of the resulting decisions. The authors derive convergence rates for both the approximate posterior and the corresponding optimal value, then illustrate the theory with three examples spanning parametric and nonparametric settings. The contribution is a framework for tractable risk-sensitive decisions together with an account of how its statistical approximations behave as information accumulates.
neurips-2023-on-the-statistical-consiste.tldr: RSVB jointly approximates a risk-sensitive Bayesian posterior and decision rule, with convergence analysis for the approximation and optimal value.

paragraphs: Online learners must make decisions as data arrives, sometimes while the rules defining acceptable decisions also change. This paper studies nonlinear constraints that vary adversarially over time. The learner does not know the feasible set in advance, and the theoretical setting allows that set to change slowly.

The proposed algorithm, Constraint Violation Velocity Projection, or CVV-Pro, relies on sparse local linear approximations of the feasible set. It therefore avoids solving an optimization problem over the entire feasible region at every iteration. This local approach addresses the computational burden associated with methods that repeatedly project onto, or otherwise optimize over, the full set.

The authors establish regret growing as the square root of the number of rounds and convergence toward feasibility at an inverse-square-root rate. The regret bound means average regret decreases as more rounds are observed. These guarantees retain the stated slowly varying feasible-set setting. Experiments also examine two-player games with a shared constraint, extending the evaluation to interacting decision-makers whose choices must respect the same restriction.
neurips-2023-online-learning-under-adver.tldr: CVV-Pro uses local constraint approximations to obtain square-root regret and inverse-square-root feasibility convergence when the unknown feasible set changes slowly.

paragraphs: A robot searching an indoor environment must cope with blocked views, limited visibility, and localization errors. The authors model this search as a partially observable decision process whose state space grows as the robot explores a three-dimensional region. This formulation accommodates uncertainty about a scene that is only partly known.

Their planner, GPOMCP, combines online Monte-Carlo tree search with reuse of a belief tree and a new upper confidence bound. Reusing earlier planning work is shown to be reasonable and effective when differences between beliefs are limited. When no objects have been detected and guidance is scarce, a guessed target object and an updating grid world help direct the search.

Evaluation uses the Fetch robot simulator in Gazebo across four target-finding scenarios in a realistic indoor living environment. Compared with POMCP-based baselines, the method finds targets faster and with higher success rates under the same computational requirements. These are simulation findings, and the result concerning belief-tree reuse specifically retains its condition that the belief differences remain limited.
neurips-2023-pomdp-planning-for-object-s.tldr: GPOMCP combines a growing search model, conditional reuse of planning work, and exploratory guidance to improve simulated robot object search.

paragraphs: Learning with Errors, or LWE, is a mathematical problem underlying cryptographic security, including homomorphic encryption. Some applications use secrets with small entries, and sparse small secrets are attractive for efficiency and functionality. This paper studies the security implications of those choices by improving machine learning attacks that recover such secrets.

Earlier attacks recovered sparse binary secrets. VERDE extends recovery to sparse binary, ternary, and narrow Gaussian secrets through improved preprocessing and secret-recovery techniques. The authors report attacks at larger dimensions, including n = 512, and at smaller moduli, including log2 q = 12 when n = 256, while using less time and power.

The work also proposes architectures intended to support scaling and develops a theory explaining why machine learning attacks on LWE succeed. Its significance is more precise scrutiny of particular secret distributions and parameter choices. The findings establish stronger attacks on the sparse, small-secret settings studied; their scope should remain tied to those settings rather than being read as a general defeat of LWE-based cryptography.
neurips-2023-salsa-verde-a-machine-learn.tldr: VERDE improves machine learning recovery of sparse small LWE secrets, extending supported secret types and attacking more demanding parameter settings.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning agents can give disproportionate weight to early experiences, a problem called primacy bias. Their neural networks may overfit to those experiences even as more data becomes available. One proposed remedy periodically resets some or all of an agent while retaining its replay buffer of previously collected experience.

Resets introduce their own difficulty: performance can collapse immediately afterward. That instability matters when evaluating both safety and the cost of poor decisions during learning. This paper proposes a reset-based method using deep ensemble learning to address the shortcomings of ordinary resets while improving how efficiently the agent learns from collected samples.

The authors evaluate the method in several experiments, including safe reinforcement learning settings, and report evidence supporting its effectiveness. The findings suggest that combining ensembles with resets can help manage the tension between escaping early-experience bias and preserving useful behavior during training. The numerical results indicate potential for applications where sample efficiency and safety matter, rather than establishing a universal safety guarantee for deployed agents.
neurips-2023-sample-efficient-and-safe-d.tldr: A reset-based ensemble method addresses early-experience bias and post-reset performance collapse, with experiments supporting improved sample efficiency and safety-related performance.

paragraphs: Sequential statistical tests evaluate observations as they arrive and allow a data-dependent decision to stop or continue collecting evidence. This paper studies tests for whether two distributions differ and whether variables are independent, while maintaining control of false rejections. It uses testing by betting, where accumulated betting wealth measures evidence against the null hypothesis.

The proposed betting strategies rely on predictors updated over time. For two-sample testing, consistently predicting which distribution produced an observation supplies evidence of a difference. For independence testing, the predictor distinguishes joint observations from observations generated from the product of the marginals through external randomization. Predictive success then provides evidence of dependence.

This approach addresses the difficulty of selecting suitable kernels for high-dimensional or structured data such as images. Experiments report better performance than kernel-based tests in structured settings. The authors also show applicability beyond independent, identically distributed observations, with validity and power maintained in time-drifting settings. The contribution links learned prediction to sequential evidence while retaining the testing framework’s control over erroneous rejection.
neurips-2023-sequential-predictive-two-s.tldr: Sequentially updated predictors drive betting-based tests for distribution differences and dependence, improving structured-data results while controlling false rejections.

paragraphs: Explanations of automated decisions often tell someone how to change an unfavorable result into a favorable one. This paper asks what an explanation should offer someone who already received a positive result. It studies semifactual explanations, which describe beneficial changes a person could make while keeping the same favorable decision.

The authors introduce Gain to express how much a user benefits from such an explanation. They also provide a causal formalization of semifactuals, bringing causal relationships into the process of identifying useful changes. The objective is to improve the user’s situation without crossing the system’s decision boundary and losing the positive outcome.

Benchmark experiments show that the proposed algorithms achieve greater gain than prior work and that causality matters in this process. A user study further finds that people receiving a loan acceptance consider semifactual explanations more useful than counterfactual ones. That result supports the paper’s hypothesis in the positive loan-decision setting: an explanation can help users make better use of an acceptance, beyond merely explaining how acceptance could be obtained.
neurips-2023-the-utility-of-even-if-semi.tldr: Semifactual explanations identify beneficial changes that preserve a positive decision, with benchmark and user-study evidence supporting their usefulness.

paragraphs: Molecular dynamics commonly advances an all-atom system in femtosecond-scale steps, while processes such as folding and binding can take milliseconds or longer. This timescale gap makes equilibrium sampling expensive. Timewarp aims to accelerate exploration by learning larger moves from existing molecular dynamics trajectories.

The method trains a normalizing flow offline to propose changes corresponding to 100,000 to 1,000,000 femtoseconds of molecular dynamics. Those proposals are used within a Markov chain Monte Carlo method targeting the Boltzmann distribution. The learned model thus supplies large candidate steps inside a sampling procedure directed at the desired equilibrium distribution.

A central result is transfer between molecular systems. After training, Timewarp generalizes to previously unseen small peptides containing two to four amino acids at all-atom resolution. It explores their metastable states and accelerates sampling in wall-clock time compared with standard molecular dynamics. These findings support transferable learned proposals as a route toward faster molecular sampling, with the demonstrated transfer specifically covering the small peptides studied.
neurips-2023-timewarp-transferable-accel.tldr: Timewarp learns large molecular sampling proposals and transfers them to unseen small peptides, accelerating equilibrium sampling compared with standard molecular dynamics.

paragraphs: Periodic materials have physical symmetries that differ from those encountered in individual molecules. A generative model must account for those symmetries when representing and producing material structures. The authors argue that existing methods do not fully capture them and introduce SyMat to address this gap.

SyMat divides generation into complementary components. A variational autoencoder generates sets of atom types together with lattice lengths and angles. A score-based diffusion model generates atomic coordinates, using a symmetry-aware probabilistic model during coordinate diffusion. This design handles the material’s composition and lattice alongside the spatial arrangement of its atoms.

The authors establish theoretical invariance to all material symmetry transformations and report promising performance in random generation and property optimization tasks. The invariance result concerns the model’s treatment of equivalent structures under symmetry, while the experiments assess its usefulness for generating materials. Together, the contributions connect a physical requirement of periodic structures with a practical generative framework, without elevating the reported promising task performance into a claim of universal superiority.
neurips-2023-towards-symmetry-aware-gene.tldr: SyMat combines variational generation and coordinate diffusion to generate periodic materials with theoretically established symmetry invariance.

paragraphs: Prompt tuning adapts vision-language models by learning prompts that influence how images and text are represented. The authors argue that using a single prompt per modality and aligning only whole images with whole sentences fails to capture the diversity of individual examples. Their framework addresses both the variety of prompts and the granularity of alignment.

The method learns multiple prompt modes to represent diverse semantic content, then aligns prompt tokens across modalities using optimal transport. Token-level matching lets it examine finer similarities than a single image-level or sentence-level comparison. Similarity between the modality-specific sets is computed through a hierarchical transport problem, linking the collection-level comparison to more detailed token relationships.

Experiments on image recognition benchmarks report stronger generalization and few-shot performance. Qualitative analysis also shows that learned prompt tokens can capture different visual concepts. These findings support the combined design: diverse prompts provide multiple semantic representations, while fine-grained alignment helps relate them across image and text. The evidence concerns improvements observed on the evaluated recognition benchmarks.
neurips-2023-tuning-multi-mode-token-lev.tldr: Learning diverse prompts and aligning their tokens through hierarchical optimal transport improves reported few-shot recognition and generalization.

paragraphs: Vision-language models perform well on many tasks, but their robustness to adversarial image and text changes remains a concern. VLATTACK studies a setting where an attacker uses a pretrained model to construct examples targeting black-box fine-tuned models. The attacker therefore works through the pretrained model rather than requiring white-box access to each downstream target.

The framework first creates perturbations separately for the two modalities. A block-wise similarity attack modifies images to disrupt general representations, while an existing text attack generates text changes independently. An iterative cross-search procedure then starts from those outputs and periodically updates image-text pairs, bringing the two sources of perturbation together.

Experiments cover three widely used pretrained vision-language models, six tasks, and eight datasets. VLATTACK achieves the highest attack success rates among the compared state-of-the-art baselines on every evaluated task. These results expose a deployment vulnerability in the studied setting: perturbations developed using pretrained models can remain effective against fine-tuned downstream systems, and combining image and text attacks strengthens that threat in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2023-vlattack-multimodal-adversa.tldr: VLATTACK combines image and text perturbations from pretrained models to attack black-box fine-tuned vision-language systems, leading the reported comparisons.
